extracted.intended_audience: newsroom editors, reporters, and media ethics professionals
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for detecting, investigating, preventing, and responding to plagiarism and fabrication in news reporting, with recommended editorial practices and disciplinary steps. Focuses on newsroom workflows (especially breaking news desks), verification of sources/evidence, and editorial oversight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not fabricate sources or facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters must not make up sources (for example, inventing a medical student, doctor, or witness) or facts; fabrication is a serious breach of standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article cites multiple removed USA Today stories in which the writer fabricated sources or other information. Examples include invented affiliations and a fabricated witness to a bombing. Fabrication can include producing false evidence of reporting (e.g., a fake audio recording). Where fabrication is found, stories should be removed and bylines may be stripped.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not plagiarize or lift material without attribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters must not copy exact words, quotes, or material from other publications without attribution or present others' quotes as if they personally interviewed the source.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author notes reporters often get sloppy pulling information from AP wire stories without credit or taglines; while sometimes technically allowed in AP member newsrooms, it is described as 'intellectually dishonest.' A common escalation is lifting quotes from expert sources and using them as if the reporter had interviewed them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify authenticity of supporting evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors and reporters must verify that any recordings, documents, or evidence of interviews are genuine and correspond to real interviews/sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the USA Today case the writer produced false evidence of reporting, including an audio recording. Editors should therefore check the authenticity of recordings and any documentation presented as proof of reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial investigation/playbook for suspected fabrication or plagiarism
rubrics_metrics.description: When a complaint arises, editors should follow a standard investigation sequence: question the reporter, probe for additional issues, and audit the reporter's work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Steps outlined: 1) Ask the reporter to explain themselves. 2) Ask, 'If I look through your work, will I find any other issues?' 3) Look through every story, searching for key phrases that might appear elsewhere and for evidence of named sources. The playbook was developed after prior high-profile scandals and is now widely known among editors.

rubrics_metrics.name: If one instance is found, search broadly for more
rubrics_metrics.description: Finding one case of plagiarism or fabrication is often an indicator there are additional problematic pieces; editors should assume and check for further instances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author states: 'Almost always, where editors find one case of plagiarism or fabrication, they find more.' Investigations commonly expand to review many of the reporter's past pieces and syndications across network publications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Close editing and process transparency to prevent dishonesty
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors should closely edit and routinely ask reporters how they found their sources and to describe their reporting process; this both discourages dishonesty and helps catch errors early.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The column recommends slowing down, talking to reporters about their work (which helps writers grow), and insisting on intellectual honesty. Close editing includes asking for sourcing details and verifying that reporters actually conducted claimed interviews.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use disciplinary documentation for low-level plagiarism
rubrics_metrics.description: For initial or low-level plagiarism incidents, editors should document the behavior in personnel files to put the journalist on notice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author suggests placing a letter in the journalist's human resources file as a low-level disciplinary step to deter repeat behavior and provide formal notice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remove/alter published stories that do not meet standards and be transparent
rubrics_metrics.description: When stories are found not to meet editorial standards due to fabrication or unverifiable information, remove or alter them and notify readers with explanatory notes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: USA Today removed 23 stories and other pieces had bylines removed or notes added; removed articles were 'accompanied by a note: "This story has been removed from our platforms because it does not meet our standards."' Transparency about removals and corrections is emphasized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reexamine editing structures to address production pressure risks
rubrics_metrics.description: Newsrooms should review and potentially revise editing workflows—especially in high-production breaking-news teams—to reduce the risk that speed and volume lead to sloppy sourcing or dishonesty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Breaking news desks are high-expectation jobs that must produce many fast stories. The column warns this pressure can contribute to errors and suggests editors should slow down, reexamine editing structures, and promote in-office mentoring/training to curb bad habits, particularly for staff hired during the pandemic who may not have integrated into newsroom routines.
